content.text: preop alternative: doxazosin 1 to 32 mg PO QD; doxazosin may be equally effective but better tolerated; start a BB only after adequate alpha-blockade.

CI: hypersensitivity to doxazosin, other quinazolines (e.g., prazosin, terazosin), or any of its components. Postural hypotension w/ or w/o symptoms (e.g., dizziness) may develop within a few hours after dosing; potential for syncope, esp after the initial dose or a dose increase. Concomitant PDE-5 inhibitor can result in additive BP lowering and symptomatic hypotension. IFIS observed during cataract surgery in some pts on or previously treated w/ alpha1 blockers. No apparent benefit of stopping alpha1 blocker therapy b4 cataract surgery. Rule out prostate cancer b4 starting therapy for BPH. Priapism (painful erection sustained for hours, unrelieved by intercourse or masturbation) associated w/ doxazosin; can lead to permanent impotence if not promptly treated. Strong CYP3A inhibitors may ↑ doxazosin exposure and risk of hypotension; monitor BP and for hypotension symptoms. Severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh Class C) not recommended; monitor BP and hypotension symptoms in Child-Pugh Class A and B. Following the initial dose and each dose increase, monitor BP for at least 6 h. If discontinued for several days, restart therapy using the initial dosing regimen. Most commonly reported adverse reactions: fatigue, malaise, hypotension, and dizziness. OD: most likely manifestation is hypotension; usual treatment is IV fluid infusion; dialysis not indicated (highly protein bound).
